summary: A definitive clinical guide to differentiating supranuclear gaze palsies from infranuclear lesions, and mechanical restriction from paralytic strabismus using the oculocephalic reflex and passive duction testing.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: The Doll's Head Maneuver (Oculocephalic Reflex) and the Forced Duction Test (FDT) are essential bedside tools in the neuro-ophthalmological and strabismus workup. While the Doll's Head Maneuver tests the integrity of the brainstem's Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR) pathway to bypass supranuclear control, the FDT identifies physical mechanical resistance to movement, distinguishing muscle/fascial entrapment from neurological paralysis.

branches: Activates CN III, IV, and VI Nuclei

sections.title: The Forced Duction Test (FDT): Indications
content: Differentiating restrictive vs. paretic strabismus
Evaluation of Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
Assessing Orbital Floor Fractures (muscle entrapment)
Pre-operative planning for strabismus surgery
Congenital Cranial Dysinnervation Disorders (CCDDs)
Brown Syndrome vs. Inferior Oblique Palsy

sections.title: FDT Procedure: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Administer topical anesthesia (e.g., Proparacaine 0.5%) followed by a cocaine-soaked or lidocaine-soaked cotton tip applicator over the insertion site.
Step 2: Use a 0.3mm or 0.5mm toothed forceps (e.g., Bishop-Harmon or Castroviejo) to grasp the conjunctiva and episclera at the muscle insertion point.
Step 3: Instruct the patient to look toward the direction of the intended movement (to relax the agonist muscle).
Step 4: Gently but firmly pull the globe in the direction opposite the suspected restriction.
Step 5: Assess resistance. 'Positive' = Resistance felt (Mechanical); 'Negative' = No resistance (Neurological).

rows: CN III, IV, VI Palsy, MG
MLF Lesion or Partial CN Palsy

sections.title: The Forced Generation Test (FGT)
sections.content: Often performed alongside FDT. The examiner stabilizes the globe while the patient attempts to move the eye. If the examiner feels the eye 'tug' against the forceps, the muscle is still receiving innervation. This helps quantify the degree of remaining function in a paretic muscle.

sections.title: Clinical Red Flags
content: Suspected Ruptured Globe (Absolute Contraindication for FDT)
Acute Intraocular Pressure elevation during testing
Severe Conjunctival Chemosis masking the insertion
Vasovagal response during manipulation
Recent Scleral Buckle or Glaucoma Drainage Device

content.explanation: Cold Opposite, Warm Same (Calorics) tests the same pathway as Doll's Head. VOR = Vestibular nuclei -> Opposite VI Nucleus -> Reticular formation -> MLF -> Contralateral III Nucleus.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: In Parinaud Syndrome, Doll's Head can often elicit vertical movements that are otherwise absent.
Wait at least 5 minutes after topical anesthesia for FDT to ensure patient comfort and prevent guarding.
Pseudo-positive FDT can occur if the patient is not looking in the direction of the forceps movement (antagonist co-contraction).
In Thyroid Eye Disease, the Inferior Rectus is most commonly restricted (IMSLO mnemonic).
A 'soft' stop in FDT suggests partial restriction, while a 'hard' stop suggests solid entrapment or fibrosis.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: FDT is typically performed under general anesthesia (GA) in children.
Note: Succinylcholine can cause tonic contraction of EOMs, leading to a false-positive FDT. Use non-depolarizing agents if FDT is planned.
Doll's head is highly effective in infants where voluntary saccades are difficult to elicit.

sections.title: Complications & Risk Management
content: Subconjunctival Hemorrhage (Most common side effect)
Conjunctival Tearing (If grasp is too superficial)
Oculocardiac Reflex (Bradycardia during traction)
Iatrogenic infection (Rare, ensure sterile forceps)

rows: Mild resistance; Eye reaches the end-point with extra effort.
Moderate resistance; Significant effort needed to move globe.
Severe resistance; Globe barely moves beyond midline.
Frozen globe; No movement possible manually.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Role of FDT
sections.content: Classic studies by Scott (1971) and later refinements in the AAO BCSC highlight the FDT as the gold standard for diagnosing mechanical restriction in orbital wall fractures. Recent advances suggest that intraoperative FDT is crucial in titrating the amount of muscle recession required in Graves’ ophthalmopathy to avoid over-correction.
